themes.theme: A hard constraint (required-and-prohibited overlap) is enforced only by a dev-mode assertion that is compiled out in production, instead of being part of the structural well-formedness check every code path relies on.
findingSummaries: `checkWellFormed` omits the required-and-prohibited overlap check, so the only thing stopping `constrainedGreedy` from emitting a prohibited edge is `assertHardConstraints`, which is compiled out when NODE_ENV === "production".
themes.remediation: Remove the overlap check as a CONTRACTS_ENABLED-only postcondition and fold it into `checkWellFormed` itself (the same function `validate` already calls), so there is exactly one place — always executed, never compiled out — that decides whether a constraint set is well-formed. Do not keep two checks in parallel; delete the redundant dev-only branch in `assertHardConstraints` for this case once `checkWellFormed` covers it.

themes.theme: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph's option-normalization predicate for priorWeight diverges from polishConstrained's acceptance predicate, so the documented refuse-never-throw contract is violated by negative finite weights that only the callee rejects.
findingSummaries: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` normalizes a non-finite `priorWeight` to 0 but passes a negative one through unchanged, and `polishConstrained` throws on it — breaking the entry point's documented "refuses, never throws" contract, and only for roster sizes where auto-polish happens to run.

The wrapper sanitizes only non-finiteness and hands the raw value to `polishConstrained`, whose own precondition also rejects negatives — the two checks were split on different predicates, so a negative finite weight passes the wrapper's filter and detonates the callee's.
themes.remediation: Delete the wrapper's separate, narrower finiteness-only check and normalize priorWeight against exactly the predicate polishConstrained already enforces (`!(Number.isFinite(requested) && requested >= 0)` → 0), removing the second, divergent definition of "valid weight" instead of maintaining two.

themes.theme: The pre-flight cost guard for repairDegrees is priced against a cost model (edges-added-based `greedyWork`) that doesn't match what the function actually does (passes × under-degree vertices scanned × a full BFS sweep each, with no memory of permanently unreachable vertices), so it admits inputs that run for hours.
findingSummaries: `repairDegrees`'s guard charges `REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR * greedyWork(g.n, k)`, built from edges-added, but repair's real cost is unrelated to that and the `while (changed)` loop restarts from the top of `under` on every successful add, re-paying every failing vertex's BFS from scratch with nothing recording that an isolated vertex is permanently unjoinable; at k<=2 `greedyWork`'s floor lets the guard admit n=35355 while the actual cost is cubic in n.
themes.remediation: Remove the `break` that restarts the `for (const va of under)` scan from the top after each successful add, so a single pass tries every `under` vertex once before restarting (passes × under → passes + under); this collapses the redundant re-scanning that the cost model was blind to, without needing a new stuck-tracking structure (which would be unsound here since reachability can improve mid-run).

themes.theme: Floating comment describing a past refactoring pattern with no current code to anchor to.
findingSummaries: Floating comment block explaining a deleted/moved code pattern ('iteration clamp') without relating to any current code in context, in lib/src/core/index.ts.
themes.remediation: Delete the floating comment block; it explains code that no longer exists at that location, and its absence loses nothing since `boundedPolishIterations` is documented at its own definition.

themes.theme: Duplicate/orphaned docstring left behind before repairDegrees, splitting one description across disconnected blocks that tooling won't associate with the function.
findingSummaries: Three consecutive docstrings (lines 199-203, 204-211, 212-219) sit before repairDegrees and REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR in lib/src/core/greedy.ts; the first, which describes function behavior, is orphaned and unattached to any declaration.
themes.remediation: Delete the orphaned first docstring block entirely, leaving the single docstring already positioned immediately before `export function repairDegrees` as the sole description — don't merge content into a new combined block, just remove the disconnected duplicate.

themes.theme: minSeparation is accepted by the constrained-graph entry point and silently has no effect, and that fact is documented only far from the call site where a reader would notice it.
findingSummaries: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph passes minSeparation to constrainedGreedy where it is accepted but ignored; the incompatibility is documented in ConstrainedGreedyOptions but the call site itself carries no indication of this.
themes.remediation: Stop passing minSeparation through to constrainedGreedy at the index.ts call site — since the value is a documented no-op there, dropping the pass-through removes both the dead argument and the need for a cross-file explanation.

gating.theme: a hard constraint the library promises is enforced only by a dev-mode assertion, so a production build ships the violation silently
gating.summary: `checkWellFormed` omits the required-and-prohibited overlap check, so the only thing stopping `constrainedGreedy` from emitting a prohibited edge is `assertHardConstraints`, which is compiled out when NODE_ENV === "production".
gating.failure: cons = new Constraints(6); cons.require(0,1); cons.prohibit(0,1); constrainedGreedy(6, 3, cons). Under vitest/dev it throws "constrainedGreedy: prohibited edge 0–1 present". Under `NODE_ENV=production node` it returns a graph with hasEdge(0,1) === true and edges [[0,1],[0,2],[0,5],[1,3],[1,4],[2,3],[2,4],[3,5],[4,5]] — the module header's promise ("prohibited edges never are") is false, with no error and no report channel. `validate` catches this case (Reason "required-and-prohibited"), and `checkWellFormed` already mirrors every OTHER validate refusal as an always-on throw (bad n, n !== cons.n, roster cap, bad k, work cap, out-of-range ids, self-pairs, required-degree over k) — this is the one it skips. The identical hazard was already closed for the sibling `polishConstrained` by the always-on `checkInputSatisfiesConstraints` (line 155), whose own comment gives the reason: "the only check was the postcondition at the end, which is compiled out in production (so a violating input came back unflagged)". The suite cannot catch it: vitest never runs with NODE_ENV=production, and no test constructs a required-and-prohibited pair against the primitive.
gating.remediation: Add the overlap check to `checkWellFormed`, beside the existing required-degree loop, so it throws for the same reason `validate` refuses: `for (const [a, b] of cons.requiredPairs()) if (cons.isProhibited(a, b)) throw new Error(`pair ${a}–${b} is both required and prohibited — call validate() first`)`. Close the theme, not the case: the postcondition/precondition split is the defect, so audit every guarantee currently backed ONLY by a CONTRACTS_ENABLED assertion (`assertHardConstraints` for the required-edge-missing branch, `assertWithinDegreeCap`, `assertDegreesPreserved`) and decide per guarantee whether it is structural-by-construction (keep as a dev postcondition) or input-dependent (must become an always-on precondition). Required-and-prohibited is input-dependent and O(#required) — the same class as the id check one line above it.
gating.invariant: For all (n, k, cons): `constrainedGreedy(n, k, cons)` either throws, or returns a graph g such that `g.hasEdge(a,b) === false` for every pair in `cons.prohibitedPairs()` and `g.hasEdge(a,b) === true` for every pair in `cons.requiredPairs()` and `g.degree(v) <= k` for all v — and the outcome is identical whether or not `CONTRACTS_ENABLED` is true. Testable by running the same inputs with the contract flag forced off (e.g. a test that stubs process.env.NODE_ENV = "production" before import, or by asserting the precondition throws rather than the postcondition).

gating.theme: an option value is normalized in one place and rejected in another, so the same input either throws or is silently ignored depending on roster size
gating.summary: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` normalizes a non-finite `priorWeight` to 0 but passes a negative one through unchanged, and `polishConstrained` throws on it — breaking the entry point's documented "refuses, never throws" contract, and only for roster sizes where auto-polish happens to run.
gating.failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(20, 4, cons, { priorWeight: -1 }) throws `prior weight -1 must be a non-negative finite number` (uncaught; `report.refusals` never populated), while buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(400, 4, cons, { priorWeight: -1 }) returns normally with polished:false and the weight silently discarded — because autoPolishEnabled(400,4,{constrained:true}) is false. Same for -0.0001. The function's own doc says "Genuinely-impossible inputs are refused up front with plain-language reasons rather than throwing", and index.ts:315 states the throw-vs-refuse split explicitly. Line 359 is the code that exists precisely to stop the optimizer and the report disagreeing about the weight (`priorWeight = active.priorHard || !Number.isFinite(requested) ? 0 : requested`) — it covers finiteness but not the sign check `polishConstrained` added at line 180. Not caught by the suite: optimizer.props.test.ts:602 parameterizes priorWeight over fc.integer({min: 0}) and optimizer.props.test.ts:579 covers only NaN/Infinity.
gating.remediation: Resolve the weight once, against the same predicate `polishConstrained` enforces: `priorWeight = active.priorHard || !(Number.isFinite(requested) && requested >= 0) ? 0 : requested` — or, if a bad weight should be visible rather than swallowed, return `refusedResult(n, [\`prior weight ${requested} must be a non-negative number\`])` before generation so the report channel carries it. Close the theme, not the case: sweep every numeric option this builder accepts (`polishIters`, `seed`, `minSeparation`, `priorWeight`) and make the builder's normalization the single authority, so no option value can reach a primitive that would reject it, and no option's acceptance depends on whether the auto-polish gate fired.
gating.invariant: For all n with Number.isInteger(n) && n >= 0 && n <= MAX_ROSTER, all k, all cons, and all options objects whose fields are any JS numbers (including negative, non-integer, NaN, +/-Infinity): `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` never throws — every rejection is reported as a non-empty `report.refusals`. Corollary that also must hold: for a fixed options object, whether the call throws must not depend on `autoPolishEnabled(n, k, { constrained: true })`.

gating.theme: a pre-flight cost gate whose model has the wrong shape, so it admits inputs that run for hours
gating.summary: `repairDegrees`'s guard charges `REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR * greedyWork(g.n, k)`, a model built from *edges added* — but repair's real cost is (passes) x (under-degree vertices scanned before one succeeds) x one full `bfsDistances` sweep each, which is unrelated to `edgesAdded`. The `while (changed)` loop `break`s out of the `for (const va of under)` on every successful add and restarts from the top of `under`, re-paying every failing vertex's BFS from scratch; unlike `constrainedGreedy`, which carries a `stuck` Uint8Array for exactly this reason, nothing here remembers that a vertex had no partner. A vertex is rejected as a partner by `distv[v] < minDist`, and `UNREACHABLE` is -1, so every isolated vertex is permanently unjoinable yet permanently rescanned. At k<=2 `greedyWork` collapses to its `Math.max(edgesAdded, 1)` floor of `3n²`, so the guard's admitted set stretches to n=35355 while the actual cost is cubic in n.
gating.failure: Build a graph of M isolated vertices (degree 0, so they sort FIRST in `under` and every candidate is rejected because `distv[v]` is -1) plus P disjoint 6-vertex paths whose two degree-1 endpoints ARE >= minDist apart, and call `repairDegrees(g, 2)`. Each of the P joins restarts the loop and re-pays M BFS sweeps. Measured (node 22, dist build): n=800 (M=500,P=50) 0.45 s; n=1600 3.13 s; n=3200 25.96 s — ratios 7.0x and 8.3x per doubling, i.e. Theta(n³). The guard admits all of these and much more: 4*greedyWork(3200,2) = 1.23e8, only 0.8% of MAX_GREEDY_WORK = 1.5e10, for a call that takes 26 seconds; the guard's true ceiling at k=2 is n=35355 (4*greedyWork = 1.500e10, admitted; n=35400 refused), which the measured cubic extrapolates to ~9-10 hours in one synchronous call. Present-day reachability: `repairDegrees` is exported from the package index and its own docstring calls out that it is public API that needed a guard; the guard exists but is not a bound. The in-repo call site (`ringGreedy` with `repair: true`) cannot produce this shape, since the ring seed is connected and completion only adds edges — so this is a library-consumer surface, not an app-reachable one today.
gating.remediation: Price the guard on what repair actually spends. Both quantities are computable in O(n) before the loop: `underCount` = |{v : deg(v) < k}| and `addable` = floor(sum(max(0, k - deg(v))) / 2) bound the per-pass sweep count and the pass count respectively, so refuse when `underCount * (addable + 1) * (g.n + m) > MAX_GREEDY_WORK` — that is an upper bound on the real work regardless of k, and it does not collapse at k<=2 the way `greedyWork`'s floor does. Alternatively (and additively) drop the `break` so one pass tries every `under` vertex before restarting, turning passes x under into passes + under; note that a `stuck` bitmap copied from `constrainedGreedy` would be UNSOUND here, because adding an edge can make a previously-unreachable candidate reachable at distance >= minDist, so a failing vertex genuinely can succeed later. Ratchet as a property test: instrument a `bfsDistances` counter and assert, over generated (graph, k) pairs that `repairDegrees` accepts, that `sweeps * (n + m) <= REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR * greedyWork(n, k)`.
gating.invariant: For every Graph g and every k that `repairDegrees` does not throw on, the total work it performs is bounded by the budget its guard evaluated: (number of `bfsDistances` sweeps) * (g.n + m) <= REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR * greedyWork(g.n, k) <= MAX_GREEDY_WORK. Equivalently: no input the guard accepts may exceed the cost the guard charged for it.

gating.theme: the builder documented to refuse rather than throw escapes an exception for a hostile settings value
gating.summary: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` is contractually the entry point that *refuses* (populating `report.refusals`) instead of throwing — index.ts:153-156 states the throw-vs-refuse split explicitly, and every other malformed input (bad n, n/cons.n mismatch, every `validate` reason, NaN/Infinity minSeparation, NaN/Infinity/non-integer polishIters, NaN/Infinity seed) honours it. `options.priorWeight` does not. The wrapper sanitizes only non-finiteness (`active.priorHard || !Number.isFinite(requested) ? 0 : requested`) and then hands the raw value to `polishConstrained`, whose own precondition rejects negatives as well as non-finites (`!(Number.isFinite(w) && w >= 0)` at constrainedGreedy.ts:180) — so a negative finite weight passes the wrapper's filter and detonates the callee's. The two checks were deliberately split so the optimizer and the report could not disagree, but they were split on *different predicates*.
gating.failure: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30, 4, consWithPriors, { priorWeight: -1 })` throws `Error: prior weight -1 must be a non-negative finite number` instead of returning a result. Same for any finite negative (-0.5, -9007199254740992). The throw only escapes when auto-polish runs at that (n, k) — so the failure is (n, k)-dependent as well as value-dependent, which is worse than a uniform refusal: n=30,k=4 throws, a large roster where auto-polish declines silently ignores the same value. Reproduced against the built dist; verified NaN/±Infinity are correctly normalized to 0 and -0 is correctly treated as unweighted, so the gap is exactly the finite-negative interval. Reachability today is library consumers, not the app: `GenerateOptions` carries no `priorWeight` and a grep for it across app/src returns nothing (F9 is deferred) — but the option is live, exported public API read by index.ts right now, not an unbuilt seam.
gating.remediation: Make the wrapper's normalization predicate identical to the callee's precondition: `priorWeight = active.priorHard || !(Number.isFinite(requested) && requested >= 0) ? 0 : requested`, or better, route a negative weight into `refusedResult(n, [...])` so the caller learns the setting was rejected rather than silently getting a 0. Ratchet as a property test over `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` with fuzzed option values asserting the function never throws for a well-formed (n, k, cons).
gating.invariant: For every options object, `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(n, k, cons, options)` with `Number.isInteger(n) && 0 <= n <= MAX_ROSTER && n === cons.n` RETURNS a `ConstrainedBuddyResult` and never throws — every unusable option value is either normalized to a documented default or reported through `report.refusals`. (Contrast `buildBuddyGraph`, which is documented to throw.)

Close the theme, not the case: sweep every numeric option this builder accepts (`polishIters`, `seed`, `minSeparation`, `priorWeight`) and make the builder's normalization the single authority, so no option value can reach a primitive that would reject it, and no option's acceptance depends on whether the auto-polish gate fired.
confirmed.invariant: For all n with Number.isInteger(n) && n >= 0 && n <= MAX_ROSTER, all k, all cons, and all options objects whose fields are any JS numbers (including negative, non-integer, NaN, +/-Infinity): `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` never throws — every rejection is reported as a non-empty `report.refusals`. Corollary that also must hold: for a fixed options object, whether the call throws must not depend on `autoPolishEnabled(n, k, { constrained: true })`.

confirmed.theme: a pre-flight cost gate whose model has the wrong shape, so it admits inputs that run for hours
confirmed.summary: `repairDegrees`'s guard charges `REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR * greedyWork(g.n, k)`, a model built from *edges added* — but repair's real cost is (passes) x (under-degree vertices scanned before one succeeds) x one full `bfsDistances` sweep each, which is unrelated to `edgesAdded`. The `while (changed)` loop `break`s out of the `for (const va of under)` on every successful add and restarts from the top of `under`, re-paying every failing vertex's BFS from scratch; unlike `constrainedGreedy`, which carries a `stuck` Uint8Array for exactly this reason, nothing here remembers that a vertex had no partner. A vertex is rejected as a partner by `distv[v] < minDist`, and `UNREACHABLE` is -1, so every isolated vertex is permanently unjoinable yet permanently rescanned. At k<=2 `greedyWork` collapses to its `Math.max(edgesAdded, 1)` floor of `3n²`, so the guard's admitted set stretches to n=35355 while the actual cost is cubic in n.
confirmed.failure: Build a graph of M isolated vertices (degree 0, so they sort FIRST in `under` and every candidate is rejected because `distv[v]` is -1) plus P disjoint 6-vertex paths whose two degree-1 endpoints ARE >= minDist apart, and call `repairDegrees(g, 2)`. Each of the P joins restarts the loop and re-pays M BFS sweeps. Measured (node 22, dist build): n=800 (M=500,P=50) 0.45 s; n=1600 3.13 s; n=3200 25.96 s — ratios 7.0x and 8.3x per doubling, i.e. Theta(n³). The guard admits all of these and much more: 4*greedyWork(3200,2) = 1.23e8, only 0.8% of MAX_GREEDY_WORK = 1.5e10, for a call that takes 26 seconds; the guard's true ceiling at k=2 is n=35355 (4*greedyWork = 1.500e10, admitted; n=35400 refused), which the measured cubic extrapolates to ~9-10 hours in one synchronous call. Present-day reachability: `repairDegrees` is exported from the package index and its own docstring calls out that it is public API that needed a guard; the guard exists but is not a bound. The in-repo call site (`ringGreedy` with `repair: true`) cannot produce this shape, since the ring seed is connected and completion only adds edges — so this is a library-consumer surface, not an app-reachable one today.
confirmed.remediation: Price the guard on what repair actually spends. Both quantities are computable in O(n) before the loop: `underCount` = |{v : deg(v) < k}| and `addable` = floor(sum(max(0, k - deg(v))) / 2) bound the per-pass sweep count and the pass count respectively, so refuse when `underCount * (addable + 1) * (g.n + m) > MAX_GREEDY_WORK` — that is an upper bound on the real work regardless of k, and it does not collapse at k<=2 the way `greedyWork`'s floor does. Alternatively (and additively) drop the `break` so one pass tries every `under` vertex before restarting, turning passes x under into passes + under; note that a `stuck` bitmap copied from `constrainedGreedy` would be UNSOUND here, because adding an edge can make a previously-unreachable candidate reachable at distance >= minDist, so a failing vertex genuinely can succeed later. Ratchet as a property test: instrument a `bfsDistances` counter and assert, over generated (graph, k) pairs that `repairDegrees` accepts, that `sweeps * (n + m) <= REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR * greedyWork(n, k)`.
confirmed.invariant: For every Graph g and every k that `repairDegrees` does not throw on, the total work it performs is bounded by the budget its guard evaluated: (number of `bfsDistances` sweeps) * (g.n + m) <= REPAIR_SWEEP_FACTOR * greedyWork(g.n, k) <= MAX_GREEDY_WORK. Equivalently: no input the guard accepts may exceed the cost the guard charged for it.

confirmed.theme: the builder documented to refuse rather than throw escapes an exception for a hostile settings value
confirmed.summary: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` is contractually the entry point that *refuses* (populating `report.refusals`) instead of throwing — index.ts:153-156 states the throw-vs-refuse split explicitly, and every other malformed input (bad n, n/cons.n mismatch, every `validate` reason, NaN/Infinity minSeparation, NaN/Infinity/non-integer polishIters, NaN/Infinity seed) honours it. `options.priorWeight` does not. The wrapper sanitizes only non-finiteness (`active.priorHard || !Number.isFinite(requested) ? 0 : requested`) and then hands the raw value to `polishConstrained`, whose own precondition rejects negatives as well as non-finites (`!(Number.isFinite(w) && w >= 0)` at constrainedGreedy.ts:180) — so a negative finite weight passes the wrapper's filter and detonates the callee's. The two checks were deliberately split so the optimizer and the report could not disagree, but they were split on *different predicates*.
confirmed.failure: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30, 4, consWithPriors, { priorWeight: -1 })` throws `Error: prior weight -1 must be a non-negative finite number` instead of returning a result. Same for any finite negative (-0.5, -9007199254740992). The throw only escapes when auto-polish runs at that (n, k) — so the failure is (n, k)-dependent as well as value-dependent, which is worse than a uniform refusal: n=30,k=4 throws, a large roster where auto-polish declines silently ignores the same value. Reproduced against the built dist; verified NaN/±Infinity are correctly normalized to 0 and -0 is correctly treated as unweighted, so the gap is exactly the finite-negative interval. Reachability today is library consumers, not the app: `GenerateOptions` carries no `priorWeight` and a grep for it across app/src returns nothing (F9 is deferred) — but the option is live, exported public API read by index.ts right now, not an unbuilt seam.
confirmed.remediation: Make the wrapper's normalization predicate identical to the callee's precondition: `priorWeight = active.priorHard || !(Number.isFinite(requested) && requested >= 0) ? 0 : requested`, or better, route a negative weight into `refusedResult(n, [...])` so the caller learns the setting was rejected rather than silently getting a 0. Ratchet as a property test over `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` with fuzzed option values asserting the function never throws for a well-formed (n, k, cons).
confirmed.invariant: For every options object, `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(n, k, cons, options)` with `Number.isInteger(n) && 0 <= n <= MAX_ROSTER && n === cons.n` RETURNS a `ConstrainedBuddyResult` and never throws — every unusable option value is either normalized to a documented default or reported through `report.refusals`. (Contrast `buildBuddyGraph`, which is documented to throw.)

observations.note: repairDegrees work budget failed twice before landing. r10 reused greedyWork (built from EDGES ADDED, unrelated to repair cost) -> r11 found it prices the wrong quantity. The intermediate fix in THIS round over-charged so badly it refused an edgeless n=1200 repair costing 35ms, which I caught by measuring rather than by review. Repair now has its own constant in its own units, calibrated against three measured points, with the accept-set asserted from BOTH sides — the second failure was a false REFUSAL, which no one-sided test would have caught.

The headline guarantee "prohibited edges never are" was enforced only in development: required edges are laid down before legalEdge runs, so a required+prohibited pair went straight into the graph and only assertHardConstraints caught it — compiled out when NODE_ENV is production.
